To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we identified 127 cancer genes across 12 cancer types, and that these genes are involved in many different cellular pathways, such as cell cycle, DNA repair and metabolism.

we have used the latest sequencing methods to analyze 3,281 tumors across 12 cancer types and identified 127 significantly altered genes, which are involved in well-known and emerging cellular processes in cancer and show tissue-specificity, and that the number of mutations in the significantly altered genes varies across tumor types, indicating that the oncogenic process requires only a small number of driver mutations.
we have analyzed somatic mutations across 12 cancer types and have identified significantly mutated genes that are likely to play important roles in oncogenesis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mutational landscapes of 12 cancer types and their implications for tumorigenesis.
identifying the genetic basis for cancer.
the identification of somatic variants across 3,281 cancer samples from 12 tumour type projects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cancer genome is complex, with many different genes being altered in a given cancer, but that there are also many genes that are altered in a significant number of cancers.
this is the most complete analysis of cancer mutations to date.
the cancer genome is a complex and dynamic entity, with many genes and pathways involved in tumour formation, and that these are not static, but change over time.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the TCGA has identified a large number of new genes that are significantly mutated in cancer and have important biological and clinical implications.
the Pan-Cancer effort is a great success.
the TCGA data are a rich source for identifying cancer genes, pathways and processes, and for understanding the genetic basis of cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a lot more to learn about how cancer develops, and that we can do it with data.
there are many more cancer genes than we previously thought and they are not all the same across all cancers.
there are a relatively small number of cancer drivers, and that these drivers are shared across multiple cancer types, but also show tissue specificity.
